entries.content:
Thomas Kurian

CEO, Google Cloud

Every healthcare organization is working to deliver great care to more people at a lower cost. However, a general AI model is not enough to solve this challenge. Today, healthcare runs on fragmented data. Patient records, coverage policies, and clinical evidence remain trapped across disconnected EHRs, claims systems, and administrative tools that don’t work together. Clinicians are forced to spend nearly 28 hours a week on manually reconciling information, and patients wait for answers about their care and their coverage.

Healthcare organizations need a single, secure, governed orchestration layer that coordinates work across the systems they already run, assembling verifiable evidence and taking multi-step workflows through to completion with human oversight.

Today, we are announcing Gemini for healthcare. This purpose-built industry solution extends the universal Gemini agent, we introduced last month at Gemini at Work. 

The Gemini agent is a single, always-on agent for work where employees delegate an objective, and the agent plans the steps, retains organizational context, and routes across the best models to deliver finished outcomes inside the tools teams already use. The Gemini agent is built with enterprise-grade identity administration, fine-grained access control, and centralized policy management directly into its runtime. Every agent operates with a distinct identity, inherits each user’s existing role-based permissions, and enforces strict need-to-know boundaries across every user, sub-agent, and workflow.

Working across clinical, financial, and administrative systems, it orchestrates multi-step tasks without forcing teams to switch applications:

  • For providers: Gemini provides a patient’s history across care settings, charts are prepared before the visit, and authorization packets are assembled against payer policy before submission, so fewer claims come back denied.

  • For health plans and payers: Gemini ensures requests are checked against medical policy and organized for the clinical reviewer, and benefits and costs are explained to members from their own plan documents.

Gemini for healthcare is built to support HIPAA compliance, with governance running underneath it all. It’s available starting today in preview.

Four components of Gemini for healthcare

Developed alongside clinical and health plan leaders, Gemini for healthcare provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for payers and providers with four core components:

  • Skills for healthcare work: Skills are reusable instructions and context, written by domain experts, that teach Gemini to run a specific task. Purpose-built, multi-step instructions guide the Gemini agent through essential clinical and administrative tasks, such as medical records synthesis, pre-appointment preparation, coverage and policy review, and payer benefit determination. Each skill applies your organization’s policies and plan rules, and teams can build custom skills tailored to the workflows and standard operating procedures unique to their organization.

  • Connectors to clinical, financial, and operational systems: A library of connectors links Gemini directly to the EHR, claims, care management, and administrative systems organizations already run. Gemini queries each system while strictly preserving existing identity and role-based access controls, so teams get unified context without migrating sensitive data or altering permissions.

  • An open healthcare partner ecosystem: Every health system and health plan runs a different mix of systems. Healthcare systems integrators and digital health partners help organizations extend Gemini with specialized solutions, connect it to what they already run, and scale it without lock-in.

  • A secure, governed platform with open model choice: Clinical, security, and IT leaders get one place to set and enforce policies that govern every agent interaction. It is built to support HIPAA compliance, with enterprise-grade access controls, end-to-end audit logging, and verifiable citations so reviewers can check where each answer came from. Because the agent supports model choice, organizations can pair frontier models from Google and leading partners for complex clinical reasoning with fast, cost-efficient models for routine administrative steps under the same governance.

Unlocking high-value workflows with skills designed for payers and providers

Gemini for healthcare takes on the heavy assembly and administrative work that slows down clinical decisions and coverage determinations.

At the point of care:

  • Building a longitudinal timeline from fragmented sources: Synthesizes EHR and external records, separates active problems from resolved ones, lists allergies, and flags medication discrepancies. Clinicians get a grounded and unified patient picture in minutes rather than piecing together history across disconnected systems.

  • Reclaiming preparation time between patients: Prepares the patient chart ahead of a scheduled visit or procedure, flagging interval events, current medications, and outstanding clearances, labs, or consents, so care teams walk in with the full picture.

  • Streamlining clinical authorization and appeals: Extracts relevant chart evidence into an audit-ready packet for review, aligned with payer policy, flagging documentation gaps before submission rather than after a denial. If denials do occur, and the record supports it, it drafts an appeal grounded directly in the clinical record and the plan’s policy.

At the point of coverage:

  • Accelerating payer review: Checks incoming requests against the health plan’s medical policies and organizes the findings for reviewers, with findings traceable to the submitted documentation and coverage policy. Clinical reviewers spend less time assembling files and more time applying professional judgment.

  • Demystifying benefits and patient financial liability: Parses complex plan benefit booklets to estimate out-of-pocket costs, track deductibles, and verify in-network status, giving member services staff a step-by-step breakdown grounded in the member’s actual plan documents. For Medicare Advantage members, it applies Medicare’s coverage criteria where a plan’s internal rule is stricter.

Open ecosystem of connectors across the healthcare tech stack

Gemini for healthcare connects directly to core clinical, operational, and industry systems via secure connectors, inheriting each source system’s existing role-based access controls and data permissions.

EHRs and clinical data integration:

  • Epic EHR: Gives authorized users read-only access to patient conditions, medications, labs, clinical notes, and specialist documentation. With no write-back to the underlying chart, clinical data integrity remains completely intact.
  • Oracle Health EHR: Surfaces read-only patient histories, diagnostics, lab results, and clinical documentation for authorized users while enforcing zero write-back to ensure data integrity for the system of record.
  • InterSystems FHIR Server: Extending beyond EHR integrations, InterSystems FHIR MCP Server provides standardized, high-performance FHIR repository management and clinical data interoperability.
  • Verato: Resolves patient identity and matches records across visits and sources.
  • Keragon - Healthcare Integrations: Provides connectivity to 400+ healthcare applications, including EHRs, enabling organizations to securely connect their existing healthcare systems through a single MCP integration.

Eligibility, claims, and pricing:

  • Optum Coordination of Benefits: Finds additional patient coverage and determines the correct order of benefits before billing. Currently in limited release and testing with Gemini for Healthcare.
  • Optum Network Eligibility: Retrieves patient eligibility and benefit details from connected health plans in real time. Currently in limited release and testing with Gemini for Healthcare.
  • TriZetto Provider Solutions: Verifies patient eligibility, coverage, co-pays, and deductibles across Medicare, Medicaid, and major commercial plans via TriZetto's vast network.
  • GoodRx: Enables care teams to discover prescription pricing and savings options, including manufacturer-sponsored self-pay programs, directly within AI-powered workflows to help patients access more affordable medications.
  • Infinitus Relay: Automates high-volume payer phone calls required for prior authorization and benefit verification.

Terminology and coding:

  • IMO Health: Brings terminology normalization, clinical search, and knowledge graphs into healthcare skills and governed agentic workflows.
  • ICD-10 Codes: Searches and validates ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes, billable status, and hierarchy.
  • RxNorm Drug Vocabulary: Looks up standardized drug names, ingredients, strengths, dose forms, and NDCs.

Coverage and provider reference:

  • CMS Coverage: Connects directly to Medicare coverage rules, National and Local Coverage Determinations (NCDs/LCDs), ensuring coverage reasoning rests on current published policy rather than static model knowledge.
  • NPPES NPI Registry: Verifies provider identity, clinical taxonomy, and practice location in real time.

Evidence based guidelines:

  • Optum EvidenceVue: Turns real-world clinical data into actionable evidence through AI-powered workflows from Optum Life Sciences.
  • BMJ Digital Health: Delivers expert-curated, structured, peer-reviewed clinical guidelines and evidence, grounding care and coverage decisions in verifiable citations.

Clinical and operational workflows:

  • Salesforce: Headless Salesforce Health Cloud integrations bring workflows, data models, and Agentforce into Gemini for governed action right in the flow of work.
  • Suki: Delivers Ambient Clinical Intelligence across healthcare workflows, transforming clinical conversations into actionable intelligence that powers documentation, coding, revenue cycle management, and clinical reasoning.
  • UiPath: Connects healthcare-ready UiPath automations and agents to help teams assemble citation-backed context for operational reviews, prior authorizations, and appeals.
  • Synthpop Careflow: Orchestrates the patient journey across referral intake, coverage verification, and patient follow-up, turning unstructured referrals into validated, payer-ready orders without manual re-entry.
  • Alteryx: Enables healthcare teams to turn their domain expertise into automated analytics workflows, grounding AI-driven insights in business rules and calculations that are visible, understandable, repeatable, and auditable.

Enterprise productivity and collaboration:

  • Sana from Workday: Connects HR, finance, and enterprise knowledge so healthcare teams can surface policies, coordinate tasks, and get work done across administrative systems.
  • ServiceNow: Tracks IT incidents, operational service requests, and approval chains while enforcing existing enterprise routing rules.
  • Microsoft 365: Integrates directly with Word, Outlook, and SharePoint so prepared authorization packets, appeal letters, and benefit breakdowns land directly in the tools where teams already work.
  • Google Workspace: Connects seamlessly with Google Docs, Gmail, Drive, and Sheets to surface internal files and coordinate administrative workflows while enforcing enterprise access controls.

Security and compliance:

  • Cyera Dataport: Integrates with Cyera for data and agent security, delivering protected health information (PHI) context to support HIPAA audits and compliance reporting.

Global implementation partners and ecosystem

Through our open platform, organizations can deploy specialized partner agents such as ASCO Oncology Guideline Assistant or work with healthcare systems integrators, including 66degrees, Accenture, Altimetrik, AuxoAI, Cognizant, Deloitte, Egen, HCLTech, KPMG, NTT DATA, PwC, Quantiphi, Slalom, Tata Consultancy Services, TEKsystems Global Services, and Wipro, to customize, integrate, and scale these capabilities across complex enterprise architectures without vendor lock-in.

Developed alongside leading healthcare organizations

Health systems, health plan providers, academic medical centers, and clinical leaders are already working with Google Cloud to shape and apply these capabilities across care delivery, plan operations, and medical research:

Synthesizing patient context at the point of care

  • “Making it easier for physicians to access and understand a patient’s medical history helps them spend less time gathering information and more time focused on patient care. Through our work with Google Cloud, we’re exploring how Gemini can interpret and synthesize complex patient information from multiple electronic health record systems and care settings, connecting data from different sources to give clinicians a more complete and cohesive understanding of a patient’s medical history.” — Michael J. Schlosser, MD, MBA, FAANS, Executive Vice President and Chief Clinical Officer, HCA Healthcare.

  • "By leveraging Gemini for healthcare, we will be able to use technology in a way that elevates the patient experience and strengthens the relationship between caregivers and those they serve. Through these integrated solutions, we expect to ease some of the administrative burden on our clinical teams and give them more time for what matters most: caring for their patients. Technology is at its best when it supports our caregivers and strengthens the human connection that is at the heart of healthcare." — Dr. John D'Angelo, President and CEO, Northwell Health.

Streamlining coverage, benefits, and payer operations

  • “The real promise of AI in healthcare isn’t simply doing today’s work faster. It’s creating a better way for the health system to work. When payers and providers can connect data, insights and workflows more seamlessly, we can remove unnecessary complexity, improve performance and help the entire system work better.” — Sandeep Dadlani, Chief Executive Officer, Optum Insight.

  • “Gemini for healthcare serves as a foundation for our unified architecture of reusable AI agents, enabling us to deliver new capabilities and productivity gains significantly faster than traditional development cycles. Our focus going forward is an agentic-AI model, where an intelligence layer drives deeper automation and operational transformation. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts is working toward that future in healthcare with Google Cloud." — Prem Somasundaram, Chief Information Officer, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts.

Accelerating clinical research and evidence-based guidelines

  • “For oncology care providers, quick access to current and relevant information is not a luxury, but a necessity. We are excited about what Gemini for healthcare could do to help care providers quickly find the critical information they need, when they need it, so they can drive better outcomes for patients.” — Clifford Hudis, MD, FACP, FASCO, Chief Executive Officer, American Society of Clinical Oncology.

Built on an enterprise-grade foundation

Google is both a frontier AI lab and an enterprise cloud. Gemini for healthcare runs on Google Cloud’s secure infrastructure and is built to support HIPAA compliance. Clinical data, prompts, and generated outputs remain within your organization’s governed environment and are never used to train or fine-tune Google’s foundation models. Outputs are grounded in clinical records, plan policies, and your organization’s approved guidelines and evidence, with traceable citations and audit logging that give clinical, compliance, and IT leaders visibility and control. And because we operate the full stack, from infrastructure and models through security and the application layer, we can optimize performance, reliability, and cost together, routing high-volume administrative tasks to fast, low-cost models and reserving high-reasoning models for complex clinical and operational analysis, so organizations can scale AI across the enterprise without scaling spend at the same rate.

This is just the beginning

The launch of Gemini for healthcare marks another step in our commitment to bring the best of Gemini to every professional and every workflow, natively tailored to the way their industry works.

Gemini for healthcare is available in preview in the U.S. today, joining our expanding suite of purpose-built solutions for legal, financial services, and government services. We invite leaders across health systems, medical groups, health plan providers, and payers to explore how Gemini can transform their most critical clinical and operational workflows.

entries.content:
Abdelfettah Sghiouar

Cloud Developer Advocate, Google Cloud

Allan Naim

Director of Product Management GKE

Over the past decade, Kubernetes established itself as the standard for orchestrating microservices and containerized applications. Today, we're witnessing the next major architectural shift in distributed computing: AI workloads moving from isolated research prototypes into large-scale, multi-tenant production fleets. In this post, we'll walk through the open-source stack that powers this shift and show you the sample manifests that you can try on your own Kubernetes clusters. You can also join us at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 to see these projects in action through live demos and technical sessions.

For modern engineering teams, production AI is rapidly moving beyond generic calls to closed, black-box APIs. Organizations are realizing that their long-term competitive advantage lies in domain specialization. Platform engineers, ML researchers, and AI builders want the autonomy to run high-performing open-weight models (such as the Gemma family). They want to adapt them to proprietary enterprise datasets by using reinforcement learning (RL) and serve them with predictable latency, high throughput, and maximum hardware efficiency.

Whether it's scientific initiatives training domain models like DolphinGemma (an LLM helping scientists study how dolphins communicate) on acoustic data, legal platforms evaluating complex contracts, or engineering teams building autonomous coding agents, the objective is the same: achieving frontier-level task performance at a fraction of the serving cost and latency.

Yet, scaling RL post-training, stateful distributed inference, and autonomous agent execution on traditional container infrastructure introduces substantial hurdles:

  • Accelerator underutilization in RL: When you alternate between training and rollout generation, expensive GPUs and TPUs remain idle for most of the training run.

  • Cache-blind load balancing: When you use standard Kubernetes round-robin and least-connections routing, multi-turn agent calls are scattered across arbitrary pods and wipe out key-value (KV) cache locality.

  • Framework fragmentation: When you operate parallel, siloed compute clusters (such as bespoke Ray or Slurm setups) alongside Kubernetes, you fragment capacity and multiply maintenance toil.

  • Agent security in multi-tenant clusters: When you execute untrusted, model-generated shell commands and scripts in shared environments, you expose clusters to sandbox escapes and privilege escalation.

At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, Google Cloud is addressing these challenges by introducing and expanding a unified, open-source AI-native stack across Kubernetes and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) based on these components:

  • OpenRL (CNCF Sandbox): A Kubernetes-native post training service that simplifies RL post-training and maximizes accelerator utilization.

  • llm-d 1.0 (CNCF Sandbox): An open distributed inference control plane that provides prefix-cache-aware routing, disaggregated serving, and multi-tier KV cache management.

  • Ray on GKE with KubeRay (CNCF Sandbox): A framework that provides enterprise lifecycle management, elastic autoscaling, and Kueue-driven scheduling for distributed Ray compute and data processing.

  • Agent Substrate (CNCF Sandbox): An open orchestration runtime that provides lifecycle management and execution targets for multi-turn AI agent workflows.

  • gVisor (CNCF Sandbox): A kernel-level container sandbox that delivers strong system call isolation when you execute untrusted agent code in multi-tenant clusters.

  • TorchTPU: A backend that provides first-class, native PyTorch support across Cloud TPUs and GPUs inside upstream vLLM and SGLang.

Bridge reinforcement learning and Kubernetes with OpenRL

While supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become standard practice, domain excellence especially in multi-step reasoning, mathematical proofing, and autonomous tool use requires RL.

Historically, it's been difficult to bridge the world of ML experimentation with production Kubernetes fleets. ML researchers want to iterate rapidly in Python and PyTorch by using standard reward functions, while platform teams need multi-tenant governance, quota enforcement, and predictable scheduling.

To eliminate this friction, Google created OpenRL and contributed it to the CNCF Sandbox.

Architectural highlights of OpenRL

  • Clean 4-primitive Python abstraction: Researchers write standard Python training code that's centered around four core primitives (

    forward_backward
    , 
    optim_step
    , 
    sample
    , and 
    save_state
    ). OpenRL translates these primitives into Kubernetes scheduling workflows without requiring developers to learn Kubernetes internals or manage infrastructure code.

  • Cooperative accelerator time-slicing: OpenRL interleaves training steps and rollout inferences on the same physical accelerators. This approach avoids the need to dedicate separate, static clusters to compute-bound training and latency-sensitive rollout generation.

  • Delta-weight synchronization: Shipping full multi-gigabyte model weights over cluster networking after every optimization step creates massive network saturation. OpenRL transmits only parameter deltas to rollout workers, eliminating rollout cold starts.

  • Zero-config dynamic resource allocation (DRA): OpenRL automatically profiles model context lengths, batch dimensions, and LoRA versus full fine-tuning configurations. It then dynamically bin-packs workloads across a heterogenous accelerator fleet by using native Kubernetes DRA claims.

Distributed inference at scale with llm-d 1.0

After you post-train a model, serving it serving it under interactive, bursty agent traffic presents a new set of distributed systems challenges. Standard ingress controllers treat LLM traffic as stateless HTTP requests, scattering sequential turns across different replicas and constantly rebuilding KV cache.

Google Cloud, Red Hat, IBM Research, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA co-founded the project, with contributions from over 500 engineers across 25+ organizations. Today, llm-d 1.0 is the CNCF Sandbox distributed inference control plane that transforms standalone inference engines (like vLLM and SGLang) into a coordinated, cluster-wide serving fabric.

Core capabilities of llm-d 1.0

  • Prefix-cache-aware routing (Endpoint Picker): The Endpoint Picker integrates into the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension, and GKE manages it natively through GKE Inference Gateway. The Endpoint Picker evaluates real-time KV cache residency across worker pods. In production deployments, it's doubled KV cache hit rates from 35% to 70% and cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 70-85% on multi-turn agent workloads.

  • 3-Tier KV cache offload: When accelerator high-bandwidth memory (HBM) nears capacity during long-context interactions, llm-d cascades KV cache blocks from HBM → host CPU RAM → local NVMe SSD / Google Cloud Managed Lustre / Cloud Storage. This offload prevents expensive context recalculations.

  • EPD Disaggregation with DisaggregatedSet: Decouples Encoding, Prefill, and Decode (EPD) onto specialized hardware pools that are connected by high-speed interconnects. DisaggregatedSet is built built on Kubernetes LeaderWorkerSet (LWS). It enables independent horizontal scaling and coordinated, zero-downtime rolling upgrades.

  • Native TorchTPU upstream support: PyTorch models run natively on Google Cloud TPUs inside upstream vLLM and SGLang through TorchTPU. Developers get day-zero parity across TPU v5e, v6e, and v7x alongside NVIDIA GPUs without the need to maintain private forks or rewrite pipelines.

  • Latency-tolerant async processing & flow control: The llm-d-async-processor component pulls background, latency-tolerant tasks from Pub/Sub or Redis into cluster slack capacity. It applies strict traffic prioritization so background processing never degrades interactive user experiences.

  • Fleet observability with Prism: Track cluster-wide throughput, inter-token latency (ITL), TTFT, and cache hit ratios by using Prism, the llm-d open-source benchmarking and performance dashboard.

Distributed Python & ML orchestration with KubeRay

While specialized runtimes handle inference and RL loops, distributed data preparation, embedding generation, and distributed PyTorch training depend heavily on Ray.

KubeRay provides an open-source, Kubernetes-native operator that manages the complete lifecycle of Ray clusters, jobs, and services (RayCluster, RayJob, and RayService custom resources) on Kubernetes.

Why KubeRay matters for platform teams

  • Declarative cluster lifecycle: Platform engineers can spin up ephemeral, self-healing Ray clusters on demand for ad-hoc training runs, or run long-lived clusters for batch pipelines.

  • Native Kueue queueing & multi-tenancy: KubeRay integrates directly with Kueue for multi-tenant fair sharing, priority preemption, and quota management across shared GPU and TPU capacity.

  • Elastic autoscaling: KubeRay dynamically scales worker pods based on active Ray tasks and actor placement, preventing idle resource consumption.

Strong isolation for AI agents: Agent Substrate & gVisor

As multi-turn AI agents advance from conversational assistants to autonomous systems that generate code, execute shell commands, and orchestrate external APIs running untrusted, model-generated code in shared clusters introduces serious security risks.

Google Cloud is contributing Agent Substrate and continuing core contributions to gVisor in the CNCF Sandbox:

  • Kernel-level sandboxing: gVisor provides a user-space kernel that intercepts and virtualizes system calls, which helps ensure that untrusted agent code can't compromise the host kernel or access neighboring tenant workloads.

  • Sub-second ephemeral execution: Sandboxes spin up in milliseconds per agent turn, providing isolated execution environments for both RL rollout generation in OpenRL and live production agent workflows.

Proven in practice: Mastering domain reasoning

To evaluate this complete open-source stack on a rigorous enterprise workload, we tested Gemma 4 against the open-source Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) developed by Harvey.ai. This benchmark spans 24 complex legal practice areas from mergers and acquisitions (M&A)M&A due diligence to contract dispute analysis. The evaluation produced these results:

  • Benchmark results: While standard SFT plateaued around 50% accuracy on multi-step reasoning rubrics, when we applied reproducible RL loops with OpenRL, we lifted model accuracy to 70%.

  • Operational efficiency: The entire training pipeline dynamically shared GPU and TPU capacity with concurrent LoRA and inference jobs on GKE without manual partition management.

How teams are adopting this stack

Connect with us at KubeCon North America 2026

Attending KubeCon NA in Salt Lake City? Come see these open-source technologies in action:

  • Join Google Cloud at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026:

  • Come say hi to us at booth #122 in Hall B.

  • Discover Googlers talks on our Google Cloud at KubeCon North America 2026 event site.

  • Attend featured sessions & keynotes:

  • Kubernetes with Conviction: How Customization is Shaping the OSS AI Ecosystem's Future - Salt Palace | Level 1 | Hall DE.

  • The Latest in GPU, TPU, NIC and Other Device Support (WG Device Management) - Salt Palace | Level 2 | 250 D-F

  • Kubernetes Solutions for Agent-Shaped Problems - Salt Palace | Level 1 | Hall DE

  • How Anthropic Almost Melted GKE (And the PRs That Saved It) - Salt Palace | Level 1 | Ballroom H

  • Gateway API Project Update: Building the Future of Traffic - Salt Palace | Level 2 | 250 D-F

  • Watch live demos at the Google Cloud booth:

  • Demo | Inferencing with ARM processors on GKE (Tue 1:30-4:30PM MST)

  • Sandbox your agent workflows with gVisor (Tue 4:30-7:30PM MST)

  • Securely running fleets of agents with OpenShell (Wed 10:30-1:30PM MST)

  • Cost optimization via GKE spot nodes & node auto-provisioning (Wed 12:30-2:30PM MST)

  • From Reasoning to Action: Arm-Powered Coding Agents with GKE Agent Sandbox and Axion (Thu 10:30-1:30PM MST)

Get started

  • Explore OpenRL: Visit openrl.dev and check out the OpenRL GitHub repository for Kubernetes-native RL fine-tuning recipes.

  • Deploy llm-d 1.0: Head to llm-d.ai to test Gateway API Inference extensions and deploy prefix-aware inference pools on your clusters.

  • Run KubeRay: Follow the KubeRay documentation to manage distributed Ray workloads alongside Kueue.

  • Deploy Gemma on GKE: Explore step-by-step guides for deploying Gemma models on TPUs and GPUs in the Google Kubernetes Engine documentation.

entries.content:
Jeanette Manfra

VP, Head of Risk and Compliance, Google Cloud

Throughout my career in cybersecurity and infrastructure protection — both in government and now at Google Cloud — I have consistently seen that friction between new and existing technology is often a barrier to progress. A new piece of software or service may work wonderfully on its own but then it’s placed within a complex, interconnected IT environment and lost in the operational inertia.

Today, enterprise technology is experiencing a historic transformation. Organizations globally are moving beyond integrating AI and LLMs, and are now utilizing AI to power autonomous, agentic workflows. Nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 are already using Gemini Enterprise to build, scale and govern agents. But as AI systems begin to plan, execute multi-step processes, and work alongside human teams, leaders are confronting this same tension between cutting-edge and legacy technology.

To understand how existing technology environments shape an organization’s ability to operationalize AI, Google Cloud partnered with Hypothesis Group to survey 1,250 enterprise IT and business decision-makers across the United States. The findings reveal a critical paradox: the legacy software systems enterprises rely on to deliver technology to their employees are simultaneously functioning as an innovation tax, actively holding back the AI transformation leaders are trying to achieve.

Legacy IT’s operational toll

In our study, we defined “legacy” technology as software running locally on computers and servers rather than natively in the cloud. Across industries, decision-makers report that maintaining this footprint exerts a constant friction on their AI ambitions.

The consequences to AI are not theoretical. Nearly half (49%) of respondents report that relying on on-premises software has actively delayed, reduced in scope, paused or canceled AI or other technology initiatives.

Digging deeper, routine patch application and maintenance emerged as a primary operational bottleneck. As AI-enabled vulnerability discovery accelerates, the rate at which flaws are surfaced in legacy codebases has outpaced what human security teams can realistically address.

This creates a zero-sum game between routine maintenance of legacy systems and AI modernization. Instead of directing engineer cycles toward AI modernization, IT teams are spending their time and resources on maintaining legacy systems.

Enterprise monoculture

Customer choice

The solution to vendor lock-in is straightforward: enterprise buyers and policymakers must ensure organizations have genuine choice and interoperability in their software, cloud and AI architectures.

Furthermore, 80% of leaders agree that a provider’s installed base should not determine which AI technology an organization uses, while 78% believe that the providers who led the previous era of enterprise technology may not be best positioned to lead the AI era. Organizations want the freedom to choose best-of-breed intelligence on its own merits, rather than accepting bundled defaults tied to legacy desktop software.

Accelerate agentic technology

Delivering this level of autonomous agility across the enterprise requires modern technology built to support the agentic era. Here are a few ideas to get there:

  • Demand architectural and provider choice: AI and cloud must never be held hostage by the legacy software running local servers, email or desktop operating systems. Organizations need the commercial and architectural freedom to select best-of-breed IT on its own merits.
  • Commit to secure-by-design foundations: The industry must move past the broken cycle of releasing insecure software and patching it after the fact. Software manufacturers must engineer durable, resilient architectures where entire vulnerability classes are eliminated before code ever ships — relieving understaffed IT teams from perpetual applying routine but necessary patches.
  • Deploy AI-driven defense to remediate legacy debt: For the millions of lines of vulnerable legacy software already running in production, organizations must shift from manual triage to proactive, AI-assisted defense. By deploying platforms like Security Command Center and Mandiant threat analytics, teams can use intelligence to continuously surface active exploit paths, prioritize critical exposure and automate remediation across complex, hybrid environments.

The promise of agentic AI is to help automate friction away, and accelerate human ingenuity. But that future cannot be built on top of software designed decades ago. As IT leaders plan their roadmaps, it is time to ask: Is your technology foundation accelerating your future, or are you paying a maintenance tax just to keep the past running?

Learn more about the research here.

Welcome to the first Cloud CISO Perspectives for November 2026. Today, Chris Betz shares our security forecast for 2027, with insights from top leaders at Google, Google Cloud, and Mandiant.

As with all Cloud CISO Perspectives, the contents of this newsletter are posted to the Google Cloud blog. If you’re reading this on the website and you’d like to receive the email version, you can subscribe here.

Our security forecast for 2027

By Chris Betz, CISO, Google Cloud

Today, we’re publishing insights on the cybersecurity trends and challenges we anticipate in 2027, including agentic threats, changing attack tactics, and the new security defense approaches required.

This year we’ve witnessed a fundamental change in cybersecurity. When the year began, only a few organizations were using LLMs and agents to find and fix vulnerabilities. Today, it’s happening at scale across enterprises.

Organizations expected a reality with agentic hacking where scale, speed and sophistication would outpace human-only response; today, we’re seeing it in practice. Organizations predicted software development at an unheard of pace; today, we’re securing software delivered in hours and days instead of weeks and months.

We have passed many milestones, and the world won’t go back — and we are all digging in to fully understand the new reality.

The year ahead promises to be challenging, exciting, innovative and will outpace 2026. In the year ahead, enterprise software will change as agility and speed provided by agentic development shifts us from a collection of static applications to a live fabric of autonomous agents that can manage pricing, negotiate supplier contracts, allocate capital, and reroute supply chains in real time.

To make this vision a reality, many organizations are rushing to build agents. It’s on us as an industry to ensure the development and operations models are designed to be trustworthy and safe.

The risks in 2027 won’t be just server outages or stolen databases. As the agentic operations world takes off, we also need to be concerned about the data and technology foundation that agents rely on.

When an agent makes a consequential decision, you must be able to reconstruct the entire story: what inputs came in, how the agent reasoned through them, which tools it called, what parameters it passed, and why policy allowed it. Without that trace, you can't debug it, you can't validate its correctness, and you can't trust it. And if you can't trust it, you can't scale it.

Karthik Narain, chief product and customer officer, Google Cloud

Security must evolve to protect the balance sheet through decision integrity. Every consequential action taken by an autonomous system requires a complete, tamper-proof decision trace, recording and tracking:

  • Inputs entered into the system.

  • How the model reasoned through its decisions.

  • Which tools the model called, what parameters it passed, and why policy allowed it.

Collecting this data will help ensure that your teams can reconstruct, validate, and audit every automated decision before scaling.

Making the alert queue disappear, from chasing tickets to setting doctrine

For decades, security operations centers (SOCs) have suffered from crippling alert fatigue — too many alerts compounded by legacy security tools that hand human analysts half-finished investigations. When autonomous threats can probe a network and move laterally in minutes, human defenders can’t manually stitch together logs across eight different consoles or approve individual defensive actions at microsecond speed.

2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.

Ramya Chitrakar, vice-president, Engineering, Google Cloud Security

That broken alert queue disappears in 2027 by flipping the operational model. The alert becomes the final output of an investigation. Autonomous defensive agents will handle the data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket.

Instead of chasing alerts at a keyboard, human analysts move up the stack to set strategic doctrine, define risk appetite, and verify automated actions built for rapid explainability — where any defensive decision can be understood by a human in 60 seconds and reversed in 30.

Moving Beyond Zero: Transaction-level trust and first-class agent identities

As enterprises deploy thousands of custom agents across multicloud environments, flat trust architectures, shared human service accounts, and blanket administrator tokens are turning internal workflows into high-leverage entry points for prompt injection and lateral movement.

Traditional Zero Trust is too rigid and broad to govern autonomous software acting on its own.

We need to extend the Zero Trust concept, not just at the network layer and the machine layer, but now down to the transaction layer.

Heather Adkins, vice-president, Security Engineering, Google

The year ahead demands an architectural shift to Beyond Zero so we can extend verification down to every individual transaction, network packet, and point-in-time authorization. Every autonomous agent should be treated as a first-class identity with its own verifiable credentials, strict least-privileged scope, and open communication standards. 

When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous.

Closing the loop between live runtime and defect-free code

The traditional divide between writing software and securing it is breaking down, while adversaries actively target the open-source libraries and external tools that coding assistants pull into codebases. Developers can no longer file a ticket and wait weeks for a manual security review, yet deploying hasty, unvalidated automated patches in production is just as dangerous to business continuity as the vulnerability itself.

Adversaries aren't just attacking model math and algorithms. They're actually poisoning the open source software, supply chain, MCP tools, and external libraries that agentic coding assistants pull automatically into code bases.

Sandra Joyce, vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence

In 2027, security becomes a closed-loop, continuous system embedded directly into the software delivery pipeline. By placing agentic reasoning inside developer tools, we can perform threat modeling and catch configuration errors side-by-side as code is written.

It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production.

Turning internal ground truth into a decisive defender advantage

Concerns persist around attackers gaining the upper hand in cybersecurity, and many fear autonomous capabilities will only widen that gap in 2027. Adversaries are already compressing six months of reconnaissance into hours, and exploiting flaws before vendors even know they exist. Compounding the challenge for defenders, no single model can discover or patch every vulnerability across code and cloud on its own.

The defender's advantage is that attackers operate with fragmented external visibility and guesswork. Defenders own the complete ground truth, identity privilege graphs, internal network architecture, code lineage, and real-time runtime activity.

Sandra Joyce, vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence

In the year ahead, defenders will use autonomous technology to capitalize on the one thing an outside attacker will never have: complete internal ground truth. While adversaries operate with fragmented external visibility and guesswork, defenders own the full picture of their identity privilege graphs, internal network architecture, code lineage, and live runtime activity.

By feeding that unified context into multi-model ensembles — such as pairing lightweight models for continuous scanning with deep reasoning models that cross-validate findings and eliminate false positives — organizations can spot and remediate toxic combinations of permissions and configurations that look harmless in isolation, before an external attacker can ever piece them together.

Countering asymmetric threat speed and the new extortion playbook

Not every adversary will embrace machine speed the same way in 2027. While state-sponsored espionage actors often avoid loud, hyper-fast automated scripts that risk triggering alarms and blowing their long-term stealth, cybercriminals tend to go all-in on autonomous velocity.

What we're seeing right now is a variety of adversaries that are exploiting vulnerabilities before the vendors even know about it.

Charles Carmakal, CTO, Mandiant Consulting

As endpoint defenses get better at blocking traditional file-encrypting ransomware, criminal crews are shifting to rapid, high-volume data theft and extortion — specifically targeting proprietary model weights, custom agent skills, prompt libraries, and cloud GPU compute (“LLMJacking”).

Preparation here means eliminating security silos. It’s a critical failure point to treat models, agent permissions, software supply chains, and cloud infrastructure as separate domains.

Instead, we want to unite them under a single, intelligence-led governance framework that allows defenders to lock down high-value autonomous assets and shut down extortion paths before data can leave the environment.

Red-teaming the agentic enterprise before adversaries attack

In the rush to capture productivity gains in the year ahead, many enterprises are deploying custom agents directly into core business workflows without testing how those systems behave under adversarial pressure. That mistake leaves guardrails vulnerable to bypasses, scanner blinding, and indirect prompt injection.

One of the things that the team's been doing over the past few years is doing a lot of red team exercises… with those agentic solutions, so that we have the opportunity to identify and fix the issues before an adversary has the ability to do that against victim organizations.

Charles Carmakal, CTO, Mandiant Consulting

Continuous, proactive adversarial red-teaming must be a mandatory prerequisite before any autonomous workflow touches production. Systematically attempting to break into agentic systems, bypass safety controls, and manipulate model behavior prior to deployment is crucial to securing the agentic era.

Critically, model safety engineering should combine the results of those tests with frontline threat intelligence on novel attack prompts and evasion techniques. Defenders can then harden classifiers and neutralize new attack techniques before adversaries can use them against real victims.

Orchestrating specialized agent teams to prevent agent sprawl

Relying on a single generalist agent to defend an enterprise will fail in 2027 because deep technical skills do not transfer across domains. For example, an agent built to reverse-engineer malware is not the agent that should reason about an identity blast radius.

As departments across the business rapidly spin up uncoordinated, standalone agents without centralized oversight, agent sprawl is emerging as the next iteration of shadow IT, threatening to derail enterprise agent deployments through inadequate governance.

Technological adoption cannot outpace architectural governance… We have to prioritize machine speed defense. Security cannot remain a manual checkpoint that slows innovation down.

Sandra Joyce, vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence

Just as a well-coordinated human team beats a lone generalist, the year ahead belongs to orchestrated networks of specialized hunter, decoder, and responder agents, each operating with its own domain depth, memory, and dedicated tools.

Succeeding at scale requires building the governance and orchestration layer first. The key here will be to establish graduated autonomy, shared state, clean handoffs between specialized agents, and a central coordinator that knows precisely when to act autonomously and when to escalate to a human.

To learn more about our cybersecurity guidance for the coming year, check out our Security 2027 video.

In case you missed it

Here are the latest updates, products, services, and resources from our security teams so far this month:

  • Empowering SOC teams with the Wiz Red and Blue agents: Red Agent gives SOC teams validated pre-breach alerts, while Blue Agent investigates active threats at machine speed, helping teams stay ahead in the AI threat era. Read more.

entries.title: Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU
entries.summary: As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers
entries.content:
Fenghui Zhang

Distinguished Engineer, Google Cloud

Weiren Yu

Senior Product Manager, Google Cloud

As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle.

We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation.

For inference, it decouples TPU compute from network backpressure and turns host DRAM, local SSDs, and Google Cloud Managed Lustre into an automated, multi-tier KV cache; and for RL, it exposes low-level DMA and DCN primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to stream updated weights from trainers to samplers. By accessing device buffers in place rather than copying or locking them, TPU Sync consistently slashes KV transfer latency by over 90% and reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) by an average of 90% for heavyweight open-weight MoE models (235B–480B parameters) in prefix-caching and disaggregated-serving workloads, compared to running without TPU Sync.

Across this shared model-state layer, TPU Sync integrates directly into existing infrastructure stacks across PyTorch (via TorchTPU) and JAX — serving as the TPU KV cache connector for vLLM, SGLang, and llm-d disaggregated serving, while providing low-level transfer primitives for Pathways and multi-controller JAX (McJAX) RL pipelines.

Understanding TPU Sync: The kitchen analogy

To understand TPU Sync’s impact, imagine a high-end restaurant kitchen. Think of the TPU as an incredibly fast executive chef working on a tiny countertop (the chip's HBM). When preparing a massive feast, the chef needs lots of ingredients (the KV cache), which quickly clutter the counter.

  • The standard kitchen (without TPU Sync): When the small counter fills up, the chef has to toss out prepped ingredients and chop them again from scratch the next time an order needs them — stalling the kitchen on repetitive prep work (prefill recomputation).

  • The upgraded kitchen (with TPU Sync): TPU Sync adds a spacious side pantry (pinned host RAM), a shared walk-in cold storage room accessible to every station in the kitchen (shared cluster storage), and a coordinated team of runners. The runners slide full prep trays directly between the counter, the pantry, and peer stations without repacking them (direct DMA in native TPU layout).

Crucially, the runners swap trays in and out while the chef keeps cooking (asynchronous, non-blocking transfers).

Key use cases for TPU Sync

TPU Sync improves system throughput and latency in workloads requiring deep context, high concurrency, multi-turn reasoning and RL rollouts:

  • Long-context AI agents and multi-turn chats: When interacting with an AI agent over an extended 256K to 1M+ token session or analyzing massive documents, the model generates a continuously growing KV cache. Instead of allowing this state to exhaust HBM capacity, TPU Sync automatically tiers older KV blocks out of TPU HBM and into large pools of host RAM (with experimental tiering to shared secondary storage).

  • Enterprise applications with heavy system prompts (prefix caching): AI serving platforms receive thousands of queries that share common instructions or documents. Rather than recomputing prefixes that the model has already processed, TPU Sync extends the prefix cache into distributed host memory so concurrent sessions can reuse precomputed KV blocks and bypass redundant prefill computation.

  • Disaggregated serving architecture (prefill/decode): In modern enterprise deployments, workloads are isolated: Compute-bound nodes process the initial massive prompt (prefill), while memory-bound nodes draft the response token-by-token (decode). TPU Sync bridges this hardware gap by acting as a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) streaming pipeline. It routes the processed context directly from the prefill nodes to the decode nodes, consistently delivering an over 90% reduction in data transfer overhead.

  • Reinforcement learning pipelines (experimental): Validated on internal RL workloads and included in the repository as an experimental module, TPU Sync provides low-level DMA and DCN transfer primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to synchronize model weights between trainers and inference samplers — including automatic resharding across different trainer and sampler parallelism layouts — to reduce the time rollout workers spend waiting on weight updates.

Breaking through the memory wall with TPU Sync

At its core, TPU Sync establishes a high-performance data transfer path between TPU HBM and host RAM, as well as across TPU hosts via the DCN. It achieves this through four key architectural advantages:

  • Layout-preserving direct DMA with in-place buffer aliasing: TPU Sync accesses the underlying JAX PJRT buffers or PyTorch tensors in place and moves slices directly between TPU HBM and page-locked (

    DmaMap
    -registered) host memory in a single hardware DMA. By keeping tensors in their native TPU physical tile layout across HBM, host DRAM, storage, and the wire, data lands ready for immediate Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) execution with no Python serialization, no layout conversion, and no user-space bounce buffers.

  • Compute-overlapped transfers: Rather than taking an exclusive lock or making an on-device copy of static KV cache and weight buffers, TPU Sync creates raw PJRT buffer aliases (

    PJRT_RawBuffer
    ) without holding PJRT usage locks so block-level transfers can run concurrently with active in-place computation, with built-in DMA pacing to keep large transfers from delaying kernel launches.

  • No XLA compilation in the data path: Because TPU Sync executes transfers and tile-aware strided resharding in native C++ outside the XLA graph, moving KV blocks or resharding weights across different trainer and sampler topologies does not trigger runtime compilation — keeping the data path fast and framework-agnostic.

  • High-bandwidth PCIe DMA and DCN streaming: Using the 

    raw_transfer
    library’s direct PJRT raw-buffer DMA pipeline, TPU Sync reaches up to 223 GB/s of aggregate D2H and H2D throughput per Ironwood (TPU v7x) host out of the 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 hardware ceiling, and streams across the DCN at up to ~192 Gbps on a single 200 Gbps NIC (or ~350 Gbps across dual 200 Gbps NICs with NUMA-aware multi-NIC striping).

TPU Sync exposes a low-level data transfer API, making it easier for developers to integrate high-speed TPU data transfer into higher-level frameworks.

Higher-level architecture

Built on top of its core transport and resharding primitives, TPU Sync provides a modular orchestration stack for distributed cache management:

  • Global KV store: A global registry that maps prompt prefix hashes to physical cache blocks, handles dynamic lookups, and coordinates LRU eviction and tier demotion.

  • TPU Sync controller: The orchestration layer that generates transfer plans, coordinates data movement across nodes, and handles lease management and recovery.

  • KV cache manager: The local execution engine that tracks block states, manages HBM, host DRAM (including 

    /dev/shm
    warm-boot persistence) alongside experimental POSIX storage backends, and executes asynchronous DMA transfers.

Figure 1. TPU Sync operates as the model-state layer on TPU, unifying TPU HBM (Tier 1), pinned host DRAM (Tier 2), shared storage (Tier 3), and multi-host DCN under a single layout-preserving DMA data plane.

Solving disaggregated serving and prefix caching

Let us take a closer look at how TPU Sync helps with some of the use cases we listed in the earlier section. By treating host pinned memory as a substantial, high-speed Tier 2 cache, TPU Sync reduces the fragmentation and memory limits of standard HBM setups.

Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregated serving

In state-of-the-art serving topologies, prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) phases are isolated on separate node pools. To prevent latency bubbles, TPU Sync bridges this gap with a highly optimized, three-step pipeline:

  • Direct-DMA offloading: Once a prefill node processes an initial prompt, TPU Sync immediately moves the resulting KV blocks into pinned host RAM via its asynchronous D2H DMA path.

  • Host-to-host streaming: The TPU Sync controller then orchestrates a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) transfer, streaming the context directly to the assigned decode node.

  • Overlapped ingestion: As blocks arrive in the decode node's host RAM, TPU Sync triggers an asynchronous H2D transfer directly into TPU HBM. This happens concurrently with active decoding computation, substantially minimizing TTFT.

Host-powered prefix caching

For highly concurrent systems sharing large system prompts or running multi-turn agentic loops, TPU HBM is not large enough to hold multiple active cache blocks. TPU Sync extends the prefix cache out of HBM (Tier 1) into substantial, distributed host RAM pools (Tier 2). Because TPU Sync transfers are asynchronous, it overlaps the PCIe DMA loading of the next required prefix from host RAM with the compute of the current request — minimizing TPU idle time between requests.

For workloads that exceed even host DRAM capacity, TPU Sync also includes an experimental POSIX storage backend (Tier 3+) that asynchronously spills older KV blocks to local SSDs or shared Google Cloud Managed Lustre storage — pairing with llm-d prefix-affinity routing on GKE so replicas can recall cached prefixes across tiers without recomputing prompts.

Sample performance results

P/D disaggregated inference result highlights:

  • Over 90% KV transfer overhead cut: For heavyweight models like Qwen3 235B, median KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds down to a flat ~230 ms.

  • Substantial TTFT reduction: Demonstrated an average of 60% reduction in TTFT for heavyweight models (Qwen3 235B) under controlled, low-concurrency testing benchmarks, and an average of 90% for 480B under low concurrency.

  • Substantial high-traffic scalability: During sustained traffic spikes, TPU Sync achieves an average of 30% to 70% increase in token output throughput for 235B, depending on traffic distribution.

Prefix caching result highlights:

  • Expands KV cache capacity beyond HBM: When heavyweight MoE model weights consume most of device HBM, on-chip memory can hold only a few long-context prefixes. Offloading into pinned host DRAM expands effective cache capacity by an order of magnitude.

  • Sustains high cache-hit rates under concurrency: Pooling distributed host RAM keeps shared system prompts and multi-turn agent contexts warm across thousands of concurrent sessions instead of thrashing HBM.

  • Significantly reduces prefill recompute: Directly bypasses heavy compute layers for repeated instruction blocks and system prompts, reducing average TTFT by up to 90% on 64K-context workloads while delivering over 50% higher throughput and a 30% reduction in P99 inter-token latency (ITL).

Please see the note1 below on the testing configuration.

Ecosystem adoption and partnerships

TPU Sync serves as the open, composable memory substrate across our PyTorch-on-TPU and Kubernetes serving ecosystem, built in close collaboration with key open-source maintainers and infrastructure partners:

  • Inferact (vLLM-TorchTPU): Co-engineered with Inferact, maintainers of vLLM-TorchTPU, TPU Sync is integrated directly via vLLM's native KVConnector interface. It powers Direct-DMA host DRAM offloading and multi-host P/D disaggregation across frontier open-source models.

  • RadixArk (SGLang-TorchTPU): In partnership with RadixArk, maintainers of SGLang-TorchTPU, TPU Sync serves as both the high-speed P/D disaggregation transfer backend and the native I/O backend for SGLang’s hierarchical cache.

  • llm-d 1.0 integration: llm-d 1.0 pairs with TPU Sync on GKE to deliver global prefix-cache-affinity routing, per-rank decode session pinning, and experimental two-stage capacity spill to Google Cloud Managed Lustre.

  • Validated by frontier AI labs and enterprises: Frontier AI organizations are already adopting our PyTorch-on-TPU serving stack and evaluating TPU Sync multi-tier architectures for production deployments — including Meta, alongside major enterprises like Wayfair, and multi-silicon partners.

Get started

TPU Sync is available today as open source with Python wheels for both PyTorch (

tpu-sync-torch
) and JAX (
tpu-sync-jax
), and is integrated with vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, and llm-d on GKE. Visit the GitHub repository to explore the architecture docs, C++ and Python APIs, and deployment guides.

We are committed to working with the open-source community to advance the model-state layer on TPU — supporting new frontier architectures, expanded storage tiering, and longer-horizon agentic and RL workloads. For more up-to-date performance results, please see our ongoing efforts on public benchmarks (InferenceX).

1. Performance results are based on internal testing conducted in July 2026 on TPU v7x (2x2x1 topology), configured with PCIe Gen5 (x16) per TPU chip and one or two 200 Gbps NICs enabled per host, running tpu-inference v0.24.0 (using JAX 0.10.2 and libtpu 0.0.42.1). Metrics presented represent average and median performance improvements observed under controlled laboratory conditions. Actual real-world performance, cache hit rates, and latency reductions will vary based on system configuration, network bandwidth, concurrent traffic, and specific user workload patterns.

entries.content:
Kavitha Gowda

Product Manager, Google Cloud

Wenzhe Li

Engineering Manager, Google Cloud, Cloud AI

Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning.

Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale.

Beyond one workload, one nodepool

Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning.

To overcome these challenges, we built GKE dynamic slicing, which decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation, dynamically stitching together TPU cubes using TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to form various larger slice topologies (super-slicing), or partitioning TPU cubes into smaller slices for multiple workloads to run inside a nodepool (sub-slicing). By enabling workloads to assemble custom TPU slice topologies on demand without having to delete and recreate static nodepools, dynamic slicing reduces job startup latency, limits the blast radius of hardware failures, accelerates recovery of workloads, and improves fleet utilization and efficiency.

Dynamic slicing delivers several key improvements for platform teams:

  • Zero-downtime topology agility: Completely eliminates the rigid "delete-and-create" nodepool cycle, allowing to dynamically stitch together TPU cubes (16 VMs nodepools) to form large TPU slices, or carve out smaller-slices on the fly as an AI workload is submitted.

  • Up to 5x faster job startup: Slashes job startup times by up to five times by instantly assembling logical slice topologies from pre-provisioned TPU nodepools instead of waiting for a slow, new nodepool deployment.

  • Improved fleet utilization: Improves resource efficiency and eliminates idle capacity by enabling multi-tenant packing of smaller workloads within nodepools. Additionally, it lets you provision partially healthy nodepools. This way, you can utilize healthy hosts that would otherwise be unavailable.

  • Up to 4.5x faster recovery and fault tolerance: Accelerates recovery by isolating large slice failures to a TPU cube (a 16-VM 4x4x4 slice topology) and swapping unhealthy cubes in one to two minutes.

  • Enhanced visibility and control: Offers comprehensive insight into potential TPU partitions (slices) within each cube, covering real-time health and usage metrics to facilitate proactive, optimized workload scheduling.

Dynamic slicing architecture

GKE dynamic slicing is offered in two forms: super-slicing, to create larger scale TPU slices that exceed the size of a single TPU cube; and sub-slicing, which provisions smaller, independent slices from a single cube.

Dynamic super-slicing

GKE dynamic super-slicing utilizes TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to dynamically connect TPU cubes (consisting of 16 VMs configured in a 4x4x4 slice topology) at the time of workload scheduling. By altering the OCS network configuration dynamically, larger slice topologies are created and tailored to the workload slice needs outlined in the Kubernetes workload manifest, significantly enhancing operational efficiency.

Super-slicing fundamentally relies on a baseline conversion of all available TPU capacity into uniform nodepools composed of 16-VM (4x4x4) TPU cubes. When a TPU slice topology is specified in Kubernetes workload YAML file, the GKE scheduler (or your custom scheduler) identifies the request and instantiates slice creation. This process uses the TPU optical circuit switch to stitch multiple 4x4x4 cubes together, dynamically instantiating the targeted slice topology and scheduling the workload directly onto the newly established super-slice.

How a 4x4x16 super slice (comprising 64 Ironwood VMs and 256 total chips) is formed using four Ironwood cubes (also provisioned as GKE nodepools). At runtime, the slice is created dynamically by stitching together the TPU network across all TPU chips in these four cubes.

Dynamic sub-slicing

Dynamic sub-slicing partitions a single, pre-provisioned TPU cube (16 VM nodepool) into smaller, independent sub-slices on demand. You can manage a single pool of uniform TPU cubes and partition them on demand. With this approach, multiple distinct jobs with completely different slice topology requirements can run concurrently and fully isolated inside the same physical TPU cube, boosting overall resource utilization and allowing you to salvage and run workloads on healthy partitions, even if a portion of the cube is unhealthy.

When a workload is scheduled, sub-slicing dynamically parses its specific slice topology requirements from the incoming Kubernetes manifest. It then locates healthy partitions within the cubes, activates the high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) network to form sub-slices, and deploys the workload onto the newly created slice. Upon workload completion, the scheduler automatically deconstructs ("deforms") the slice and returns the partitions to the shared pool, making them immediately available for future workloads without having to recreate the GKE nodepool.

How GKE sub-slicing dynamically partitions a 16-host TPU cube into smaller, independent slices (e.g., 2x2x4 with 16 chips down to 2x2x2) for optimal utilization of TPU resources.

Customer use cases

You can leverage dynamic slicing to form massive TPU slice topologies to meet large scale training, ranging from large 8,000-chip single slices to multi-slices of multiple thousands of chips, down to single-host four-chip configurations. This supports a wide variety of heterogeneous AI workloads within the same environment. Designed for the demands of largest-scale workloads, dynamic slicing delivers resiliency and operational efficiency for AI workloads running across thousands of accelerators. Sub-slicing offers the versatility to efficiently scale inference workloads ranging from small to large-scale deployments.

Dynamic slicing scheduler for GKE

GKE provides deployable schedulers optimized for dynamic slicing, or you can use your own custom scheduler to manage workload placement. This flexibility allows for intelligent workload scheduling based on proactive health status monitoring. See more in our documentation.

Getting started

Pre-provision nodepools

To get started, you must perform a one-time activity of pre-provisioning TPU capacity into nodepools of 16 VMs each (maps to a TPU cube or sub-block). This baseline conversion allows for dynamic stitching of these units into custom slice topologies on demand.

Dynamic slicing introduces a new type of nodepools called an incremental provisioning nodepool. An incremental provisioning nodepool is a fault-tolerant model that supersedes the traditional "all-or-nothing" approach for creating TPU slices. GKE provisions the nodepool using all available healthy hosts even if some hosts in a 4x4x4 (16 VM) slice are faulty. The system continuously reconciles state, automatically adding pending nodes once faulty hosts recover.

This setup is a prerequisite for dynamic sub-slicing, as it allows the high-speed ICI network mesh to be dynamically configured. By using incremental provisioning, you can create nodepools for your entire capacity at once, reducing operational toil and maximizing TPU utilization by enabling sub-slicing on healthy nodes.

Workload scheduling on dynamic slicing

After enabling the slice controller in the GKE cluster and configuring the GKE scheduler, you can indicate the need for dynamic slices for your workloads using simple workload annotations.

Upon detecting these annotations, the scheduler automatically triggers the GKE slice controller to create a Slice Custom Resource (CR) to form the dynamic slice at runtime. Once the slice is formed, the workload is scheduled on the dynamic slice. Refer to documentation for examples.

Repair

When host or network failures disrupt workloads, the GKE scheduler maintains resilience and continuous operation through targeted recovery strategies:

  • Super-slicing (slices larger than 1 TPU cube): Hardware failures are isolated to a smaller unit — the TPU "cube" — allowing the scheduler to quickly reform the slice by removing the unhealthy cube and choosing all healthy cubes.

  • Sub-slicing: Slices on faulty infrastructure are dynamically reformed using available healthy partitions.

Next steps

Dynamic slicing (super-slice and sub-slice) is available for  TPUs and is offered in all regions where TPUs are available. It is supported exclusively in TPU All Capacity under reservation mode. For  working examples of dynamic slicing, refer to the documentation.
